newsitem.title: UK: Metals Outlook - More gains seen as stocks erode.
newsitem.headline: Metals Outlook - More gains seen as stocks erode.

text.p: Industrial metals prices began the week on an uptrend after new falls in warehouse stocks, although analysts say the extent of the rally may depend on how far it attracts the interest of the investment funds.
London Metal Exchange (LME) stocks of copper, aluminium, and zinc all showed drawdowns on Monday, boosting prices in early trading.
"It is plain to see that for all metals the current stock situation is markedly tighter than 1993," Nick Moore of the Flemings Global Mining Group said.
Copper -- the flagship metal -- was above $2,400 a tonne and seen heading for $2,440, the nine-month high reached in March.
"Overall, things are a bit more bullish, and the economic outlook is good," said William Adams of LME trader Rudolf Wolff and Co.
Analysts also see zinc extending upwards from its 4-1/2 year highs and aluminium building on six-week peaks.
Because the macro-economic indicators look good, and the more narrowly focused inventory data shows drawdowns, speculative investment money is swinging towards the metals.

"Right now, the move higher in prices is backed by a 'weight of speculative money' argument, but it is fair to say that in real terms there is more available to shift into the commodity markets than at any other time in their history," brokers GNI Ltd said.
Last week, LME copper stocks rose by 4,425 tonnes -- a consequence of recent high spot metal premiums sucking in metal.
But on Monday, the LME reported that stocks had fallen by 1,750 tonnes, and traders expected further inventory drawdowns to become the norm.
Aluminium stocks consistently declined last week, dropping 14,275 tonnes, and this pattern was maintained on Monday, with another 2,600 tonnes removed.

As well as the LME warehouse stock figures, the International Primary Aluminium Institute (IPAI) reports March producer inventories on Monday, and analysts are looking for further stock erosion to take place.
Most significantly, the ratios of stocks to consumption are contracting, notably in aluminium and zinc but also in the other metals.
Ratios range from 9.5 weeks' consumption for nickel to a miserly 2.4 weeks for copper -- below its critical level of four weeks.

"Aluminium and zinc are by our assessment just a week away from what could be considered critical levels (seven weeks). Below these levels prices stand an odds-on chance of getting super-heated," Moore said.
Brokers Macquarie Equities Ltd noted that strong first quarter demand was boosted by re-stocking, although this was not as excessive as in early 1994.
"This leaves us confident that growth will continue through the rest of 1997, albeit at a slower rate than in the first quarter," Macquarie said.
